rows.stem:
Observe the given figure and answer the following questions : (Any two)
(i) What is the charge on AgI colloidal particles ?
(ii) What is the reason for the origin of the charge on AgI ?
(iii) If KI is added to \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\), what will be the charge on AgI colloidal particles ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the stem is 'Observe the given figure' and sub-parts (i) and (ii) ask for the SIGN of the charge on the AgI sol and the reason for it, both of which depend entirely on which reagent is present in excess; the stem states neither, and sub-part (iii) asks the opposite case explicitly, so the two cannot be the same. The drawing is a single test tube of stippled solution: one labelled reagent is arrowed vertically downwards into the mouth of the tube from above, and the other label sits to the right with a horizontal arrow pointing at the tube's contents. WHICH label is on which arrow is the discrimination the question tests and is deliberately withheld from this note. Page idx 2.
rows.solution:
(i) The particles carry a NEGATIVE charge — the sol is written \(\mathrm{AgI}/\mathrm{I^-}\).

(ii) Because of PREFERENTIAL ADSORPTION of IODIDE IONS.

A freshly formed precipitate adsorbs, from the solution around it, the ion it has in COMMON with its own lattice. Here silver nitrate has been added to potassium iodide, so the IODIDE is in excess, and the silver iodide particles take up \(\mathrm{I^-}\) ions on their surface. Those adsorbed ions give the particles their negative charge.

The charge is what keeps the sol stable: like-charged particles repel one another and so cannot come together and settle.

(iii) The charge would be POSITIVE — the sol would be \(\mathrm{AgI}/\mathrm{Ag^+}\).

Reversing the order of addition reverses which reagent is in excess. Adding potassium iodide TO silver nitrate leaves the SILVER ion in excess, so the particles adsorb \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) instead.

The lesson is that the sign of the charge is decided by WHICH REAGENT IS IN EXCESS, not by the substance precipitated. The same silver iodide gives a negative sol one way round and a positive sol the other.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C} - \mathrm{CHO}\) does not undergo aldol condensation. Why ?
(ii) Distinguish between Acetophenone and Benzophenone with the help of a chemical test.
rows.solution:
(i) Because it has NO \(\alpha\) HYDROGEN.

An aldol condensation begins with a base removing a hydrogen from the carbon NEXT TO the carbonyl, giving the enolate that then attacks a second molecule. Without such a hydrogen the first step cannot happen at all.

In \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CHO}\) the \(\alpha\) carbon is bonded to THREE METHYL GROUPS and to the carbonyl carbon — four carbons in all, with no hydrogen left on it. So no enolate can form and no aldol follows.

What such an aldehyde does instead, with concentrated alkali, is the CANNIZZARO REACTION — disproportionating into the alcohol and the carboxylate. Benzaldehyde and methanal behave the same way, and for the same reason.

(ii) Use the IODOFORM TEST. Warmed with iodine and sodium hydroxide, ACETOPHENONE gives a YELLOW PRECIPITATE of iodoform; BENZOPHENONE gives none.

The test responds to a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group. Acetophenone, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\), has one — the methyl's three hydrogens are replaced by iodine and the bond to the carbonyl is then cleaved. Benzophenone, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COC_6H_5}\), carries a phenyl group on each side of its carbonyl and has no methyl at all.

Tollens' reagent would NOT distinguish them: both are ketones and neither responds.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the electronic configuration of \(d^4\) on the basis of crystal field splitting theory if \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} > \mathrm{P}\).
(ii) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is an inner orbital complex whereas \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}}\) is an outer orbital complex.
(Atomic number : Co = 27, Ni = 28)
(iii) Write the number of ions produced from the complex \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_6]Cl_4}\) in solution.
rows.solution:
(i) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^4\,e_g^0\).

An octahedral field splits the d orbitals into a lower set of three and an upper set of two, separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron chooses between promotion to the upper set, costing \(\Delta_0\), and pairing in the lower set, costing the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

With \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\) — a STRONG FIELD — PAIRING is the cheaper option, so the fourth electron pairs up in the lower set rather than going upstairs. TWO unpaired electrons remain: a LOW SPIN complex with \(\mu = 2{\cdot}83\) B.M.

(ii) Because the two ions have different NUMBERS of d electrons, not because the ligand differs — ammonia is the ligand in both.

\(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Ammonia is a strong field ligand and pairs all six into the lower set as \(t_{2g}^6\), which FREES TWO INNER \(3d\) orbitals. With the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) these give \(d^2sp^3\), so the complex is an INNER ORBITAL one — and diamagnetic.

\(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\). Eight electrons in five orbitals must sit as three pairs and two singles WHATEVER the ligand does — there are simply not enough vacancies to pair them further, so no inner \(3d\) orbital can be freed. Bonding must reach OUTWARDS to the \(4d\) set, giving \(sp^3d^2\) and an OUTER ORBITAL complex, paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons.

The same ligand therefore gives opposite answers, because \(d^8\) is the configuration where field strength cannot change the count.

(iii) FIVE ions. The six ammines are ligands and stay with the platinum; all four chlorides lie outside:
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_6]Cl_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_6]^{4+}} + 4\mathrm{Cl^-}\)

One complex cation plus four chlorides. The charge on the cation confirms platinum as \(+4\), the ammines being neutral.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate the spin only magnetic moment of the complex \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\). (Atomic number of Fe = 26)
(ii) Which out of the following two complexes is more stable and why ?
\(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\), \(\mathrm{[Co(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\)
(iii) Write the IUPAC name of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\)
rows.solution:
(i) Iron is atomic number 26, and water is a neutral ligand in an ion of charge \(+2\), so iron is \(+2\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\).

WATER is a WEAK field ligand and cannot force pairing, so the six electrons spread out as far as Hund's rule allows — one pair and FOUR unpaired:
\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24}\)

\(\mu = 4{\cdot}90\ \mathrm{B.M.}\)

With cyanide, a strong field ligand, the same ion would pair all six and the moment would be zero — which is why \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) is diamagnetic.

(ii) \(\mathrm{[Co(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\) is the more stable, because of the CHELATE EFFECT.

The oxalate ion is BIDENTATE, binding the cobalt through two oxygens at once and closing a five-membered ring; three of them close three rings. Fluoride is monodentate and closes none.

Two reasons: once one donor atom has attached, the second is held close to the metal and binds readily, whereas a separate ligand would have to arrive from solution; and releasing a chelating ligand requires TWO bonds to break at once rather than one.

(iii) The two ammine ligands are neutral and the two chlorido ligands give \(-2\); the complex is NEUTRAL, so platinum must be \(+2\). Ligands are named in alphabetical order:
DIAMMINEDICHLORIDOPLATINUM(II)

There is no counter ion to name and no \(-\mathrm{ate}\) suffix, which belongs only to anionic complexes. This compound's CIS isomer is cisplatin, the anticancer drug.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their property indicated :
(i) Acetaldehyde, Benzaldehyde, Acetophenone, Acetone (Reactivity towards HCN)
(ii) \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHCOOH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(Br)COOH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2COOH}\) (Acidic strength)
(iii) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) (Boiling point)
rows.solution:
(i) Increasing reactivity towards hydrogen cyanide:
ACETOPHENONE < BENZALDEHYDE < ACETONE < ACETALDEHYDE

Nucleophilic addition begins with cyanide attacking the carbonyl carbon, so reactivity falls as that carbon is made less positive and more crowded. Both ALKYL and ARYL groups do this, but a phenyl group does it far more strongly — it DELOCALISES the carbonyl \(\pi\) system into the ring, relieving the carbon of positive charge, and the flat ring is bulky besides.

So the two AROMATIC compounds come first, acetophenone below benzaldehyde because it carries a methyl group as well as the ring. Then the two ALIPHATIC ones, acetone with two alkyl groups below acetaldehyde with one.

(ii) Increasing acidic strength:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHCOOH} < \mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2COOH} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(Br)COOH}\)

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the carboxylate anion. BROMINE withdraws electron density and stabilises it; the ISOPROPYL group releases density and destabilises it, so the unbrominated acid is weakest.

Between the two brominated acids the DISTANCE decides. An inductive effect falls off sharply along a chain, so bromine on the \(\alpha\) carbon — immediately next to the carboxyl — is far more effective than bromine on the \(\beta\) carbon one place further away.

(iii) Increasing boiling point:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} < \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

All three are of comparable molar mass, so the order is set entirely by INTERMOLECULAR FORCES. Ethanal has a polar carbonyl but no \(\mathrm{O-H}\), so only dipole-dipole attraction (293 K). Ethanol has one \(\mathrm{O-H}\) and hydrogen bonds in an open chain (351 K). Ethanoic acid forms TWO hydrogen bonds between each pair of molecules, locking them into a DIMER, and boils highest (391 K).

rows.stem:
Write the Nernst equation and calculate the emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Zn} \,|\, \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\,(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \,\|\, \mathrm{Cd^{2+}}\,(0{\cdot}01) \,|\, \mathrm{Cd}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -\,0{\cdot}76\ \mathrm{V}\)
\(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cd^{2+}/Cd}} = -\,0{\cdot}40\ \mathrm{V}\)
(log 10 = 1)
rows.solution:
Read the cell diagram: zinc is on the LEFT and so is the anode, oxidised; cadmium ions are reduced at the right.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = -0{\cdot}40 - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}36\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{Cd^{2+}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{Cd}\), so \(n = 2\). Both metals are solids and do not enter the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cd^{2+}}]}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}36 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{0{\cdot}01}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}36 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log 10 = 0{\cdot}36 - 0{\cdot}0295\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}3305\ \mathrm{V}\)

The direction of the shift is the check. The PRODUCT ion is ten times more concentrated than the reactant ion, which opposes the forward reaction by Le Chatelier's principle — so the measured emf must come out BELOW the standard value, as it does.

Note also that both coefficients are 1 here, so neither concentration is raised to a power — unlike a cell whose ions carry different charges.
